steps: Site & clearances

Freestanding space heater; the label says not in any fireplace and not in a sleeping room. Hold the lettered clearances in the p. 10 diagram; reduce them only by means the regulatory authority approves.

Consult the authority having jurisdiction about a permit before installing (p. 1). The stove is meant forinsulated, habitable rooms, not a concrete, uninsulated basement or a shop/garage (p. 21).

Wall, corner and ceiling clearances are lettered dimensions (A–L) keyed to the diagram on p. 10; the residential(roof or wall exit) and mobile-home (roof exit only) rows carry the same values. In Canada, single wall pipe needs 18" clearance.

Note: the certification label says the stove is "not to be installed in any fireplace" (p. 4); p. 15 bars alcove or fireplace installs in Canada only and, for the USA, says to adhere to minimum safe clearance dimensions.
Floor protection
On a combustible floor, use a non-combustible floor shield: min. 35" x 43.125" (USA) or 47" x 53.125" (Canada); USA: 16" out in front and 8" out either side of the loading door.
Combustion air
In tight homes, plan a fresh air intake into the stove room; balance intake air against HRVs, air handlers, range hoods, dryers and other exhausting appliances.
Connector & chimney

8" 24 MSG steel connector (no aluminum or galvanized) to a UL-103HT / CAN/ULC-S629 chimney or a lined, code-approved masonry chimney. Screw every joint; support package at ceilings, listed thimble through combustible walls.

• A chimney connector is required; don't install the chimney directly at the outlet. Keep it direct, and never through anattic, roof space, closet, concealed space, floor or ceiling.
  • Never connect to a flue serving another appliance (voids warranty) or to air distribution ductwork.
  • Prefab: all components from the same chimney maker. Inside the dwelling is recommended; if it runs up the outside, build a chase.
  • Masonry: inspected by a certified professional, no cracks, loose mortar, deterioration or blockage, and cleaned first.A stainless steel liner, preferably insulated, is recommended (p. 13).
  • Maintain an effective vapor barrier where the chimney penetrates the exterior. Canada: CSA B365-M87.
Chimney height
15 ft minimum, stove top to termination, at 0 - 1000 ft; more with elevation and elbows; one offset max. At least 3ft above the roof penetration and 2ft above anything within 10ft.
Mobile home & fan power

Mobile home: Outside Air Kit + Fan Kit or Rear Shield, roof exit only, double wall close clearance pipe, stove fastened down. Fan kit: grounded three-hole receptacle; no cord in front of or under the stove.

Fit the kits before the stove. Fasten the stove to the floor (tie-downs in the Outside Air Kit): S.ZR8039 Leg Anchor Kitfor the Parlor Leg Kit; #10 screws and washers through the two pedestal base holes; #10 screws and the firebox crate'sshipping brackets for the Classic Base (p. 16).

The fresh air hose must feed up into the intake channel: it must never penetrate a wall higher than the bottom of theintake air channel on the rear of the stove, and must be kept open. Keep the floor, wall and roof structure intact. Thechimney must be removed to transport the building. Not in a bedroom or any area used for sleeping.

Fan kit: don't cut or remove the grounding prong.
Fit a base kit
Install the Parlor Leg, Classic Base or Ultra Pedestal kit before connecting the chimney. Lean the stove back with cardboard in the firebox to support the bricks.

Parlor Leg Kit S.Z1713 (3/4" wrench)

Lean the stove back onto the main air tube; fit each leg using the alignment holes and the kit hardware; stand it up;level it with the bolts at the bottom of each leg.

Classic Base Kit S.Z4815 (7/16" and 3/4" wrench)

Thread in the two 1/2" x 1/2" long bolts, leaving about 1/4" of thread showing; slide the base slots onto them; snug thetwo 1/4-20 x 1/2" bolts, then the 1/2" x 1/2" bolts; stand it up.

Ultra Pedestal Kit S.Z3903 (7/16" wrench)

Remove the ash channel seal (1/4" nut); thread all four 1/4"-20 button head cap screws halfway in; remove the ash drawer(and rear panel if needed); hang the pedestal on the screws by its key holes and slide it down; fully tighten all four;stand it up; refit the drawer.

Use extreme caution when tipping the stove, to avoid injury or damage to the floor or stove.
Hang the door
Door S.Z4886: seat the bottom hinge hole on the bottom pin, then the top, and lower until the hinge surfaces meet. The door is heavy. Never operate with the door off or left open.
Hand over
Complete the installer details on the last page (dealer, installer, date installed, serial no.) and leave the manual with the homeowner.

Thermostat set too high → lower it

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
Build the fire right on the bottom bricks (no grate) and stay with it until it's going.

  1. Check that the bricks are in place. Thermostat to High; fan off.
  2. Open the bypass, then the loading door.
  3. Put 10 balls of non-glossy paper toward the front and crisscross 20 pieces of kindling on top, leaving air gaps.
  4. Light it with the door cracked open. When the kindling is fully burning, add two or three medium logs and keep the door unlatched while they catch.
  5. Once the logs burn, latch the door; leaving it open can wear out the combustor early. When the combustor temperature starts to climb, close the bypass.
  6. When nearly all the wood is burning and the thermometer reads Active, open the bypass and door, finish loading with the wood as far back as possible, latch the door and close the bypass.
  7. Leave it on High until the fire is well established, then turn the thermostat down gradually. If the needle drops to Inactive, turn it back up.
Note: p. 25 says to "turn fan(s) on to high" as you close the bypass, then to turn the fan "on after the initial warm up"; p. 21 says fans should stay off until the stove reaches normal operating temperatures.
First fire: the curing paint gives off a strong smell and some smoke. Burn at a low setting for several hours with a door or window open.

reload.title: Reloading the stove
reload.html:
Look at the catalytic thermometer first. If the needle is still in the Active zone, use these steps. If it has dropped to Inactive, start over with the lighting steps.

  1. Have the next load ready. Turn the thermostat to High and wait a few minutes for the airflow to settle.
  2. Open the bypass and wait a few more minutes. This cuts down on smoke in the room.
  3. Crack the loading door open to let room air in; give it about a minute.
  4. Open the door slowly and reload. If smoke spills out, close the door a little so the chimney draws again.
  5. Latch the door and close the bypass right away. Leave it on High until the fire is well established, then turn the thermostat down.

On low settings you may see very little flame. If the needle stays in the Active zone, the burn is continuing.

When to reload: the thermometer helps, but also go by how much wood is left and whether the room is cooling. Don't be afraid to fill it: a full load burns no hotter than the thermostat is set.
Mild weather: the chimney draws less, so smoke may spill when you open the door. Run on High for 30 minutes after each start-up or reload, and build smaller, hotter fires instead of turning the thermostat way down.

controls.title: Bypass, thermostat & thermometer
controls.html:
Bypass handle (right side)

It opens a door inside the top of the firebox so smoke can skip the catalytic combustor. Pointing forward means open. To close it, turn it clockwise until it points to the back, then push down until you hear a click.

Thermostat knob (upper right rear corner)

High gives the most heat; turn it counter clockwise for less. Make changes gradually, since a fast change can make the thermostat work poorly. The factory-set minimum burn rate must not be altered.

Catalytic thermometer (on top)

It shows whether the combustor is working. Keep the needle in the Active zone. Inactive means the combustor is below 500F and isn't burning clean. For the most accurate reading, turn the fan off first.

Note: p. 23 says to turn the fan off for about 5 minutes before reading the thermometer; pp. 34 and 40 say to have it off for 10 minutes.
Note: p. 34 gives owner steps to clean the thermometer probe and re-align the needle, then says any thermostat or thermometer maintenance must be done by a certified installer.

Optional fan: match its speed to the thermostat setting, low with low and high with high.

wood.title: Choosing your wood
wood.html:
Burn only natural, seasoned cord wood with a moisture content of 20% or lower. Split it, stack it so air reaches every part, and keep it out of rain and snow for at least 24 months.

Hardwood and softwood both burn well in this stove; denser hardwood burns a little slower and longer. Wet wood wastes heat and builds creosote.

Never burn wet, green or unseasoned wood. Burning it can cause excessive creosote buildup, and if the creosote ignites, it can cause a chimney fire that may result in a house fire and serious bodily harm. Burning air-dried, seasoned wood lowers the risk of chimney fires and gives higher efficiency and lower emissions.

Check it with a moisture meter

  1. Pick three logs at random and split each one down the middle.
  2. On each split face, take three readings: 2" from each end and one in the middle, pins in line with the grain.
  3. Average the readings for an approximate moisture level.

Never burn

Wet, green or unseasoned wood (it builds creosote and can cause a chimney fire), salt-water driftwood (it corrodes the stove and voids the warranty), treated wood, coal, charcoal, colored paper, cardboard, solvents or garbage (burning these may release toxic fumes and/or carbon monoxide, which may result in poisoning), and flammable fluids such as gasoline, naphtha or engine gel. Never use chemicals or fluids such as gasoline-type lantern fuel, kerosene or charcoal lighter fluid to start or freshen up a fire. Doing so may lead to over-firing, resulting in a house fire and serious bodily harm.

Burning lots of lumber off-cuts, pressed logs or small, very dry pieces can overheat the stove and permanently damage the firebox and combustor.

combustor.title: Caring for the combustor
combustor.html:
The catalytic combustor burns the smoke so the stove runs clean. A healthy one keeps the needle in the Active zone (over 500 F) and often goes past 1000 F.

Check it

  • Look at it at least three times each heating season for wear. You don't need to remove it.
  • With the fire settled, open the bypass for a few minutes and watch the chimney smoke, then close it. There may be much more smoke with the bypass open.

Test it

After a well-established fire has burned for 1 hour, set the thermostat to medium-low and check the needle 5 minutes later. Repeat for at least 3 burn cycles. Still Inactive? Clean it, then retest; if that fails, ask your dealer about a replacement. The thermometer itself could be at fault.

Clean it (only when cool)

Lift off the flame shield and brush the face with a soft paint brush, or pass a vacuum wand near it. Don't scrape it, poke the cells or remove it. A hot fire is usually the best cleaner.

Never run the stove without the combustor or the flame shield in place.

Part numbers: the combustor supplied with the stove is Blaze King part # S.CAT40, listed as the combustor assembly in the replacement parts (pp. 31, 42). The certification label gives 115-1510-C2 as the combustor's OEM part number (p. 4).

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
The best way to keep the glass clean is to burn hot for a while after each reload. A fresh load gives off moisture that leaves creosote on the glass, and burning hot early drives it off. Leaving the thermostat higher for 30 minutes to an hour before turning it to low for the night also helps.

Long stretches on a very low setting leave deposits on the glass. Run it on High for about 30 minutes to burn most of them off.

Cleaning by hand

  • Only when the stove and glass are cool, never while hot.
  • Use a soft cloth and no abrasive cleaners.
  • Rinse well with water after any cleaner, or the residue bakes on and is very hard to remove.
Don't strike the glass or slam the door, and don't use the stove if the glass or its gasket is broken. The warranty covers thermal breakage only, not glass that's been struck or cleaned with harsh or abrasive cleaners.

ash.title: Removing ashes
ash.html:
Take ashes out whenever they come within one inch of the door opening. Don't empty it completely: wood burns best on a bed of ash about 1/2" thick.

  1. Make sure the fire is out and the stove is cool to the touch.
  2. Put the ashes in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid, and nothing else in it.
  3. Set the closed container on a noncombustible floor or on the ground outside, well away from anything that can burn.
  4. If you'll bury or spread the ashes, keep them in the closed container until every cinder is completely cool.
Never store hot ashes in a garage or basement. Hot ashes give off carbon monoxide and flammable gases that can suffocate you. Hot ash in a vacuum bag can also melt the vacuum and start a fire.

After the last fire of the season, remove all the ash from the firebox and the ash drawer, if you have one.

chimney.title: Chimney care & chimney fires
chimney.html:
Slow fires make tar and vapors that condense in the cooler chimney as creosote. If it ignites, it burns extremely hot. Hotter fires leave less of it.

  • Inspect the flue pipe and chimney regularly through the heating season until you know how often it needs cleaning.
  • Have the chimney and the stove cleaned at least once a year, or as often as needed. A professional chimney sweep is recommended.
  • Open the bypass before sweeping so soot and creosote fall into the firebox.
  • In extremely cold weather, water vapor can freeze in the chimney and block it. Run the stove on High for 5 to 10 minutes to melt any ice.

If a chimney fire starts

  1. Turn the thermostat knob fully counter clockwise and make sure the loading door and bypass door are closed.
  2. Call the fire department.
  3. Check the chimney, attic and roof for anything hot enough to catch fire; use a fire extinguisher or garden hose if needed.
  4. Don't use the stove again until you're sure the chimney isn't damaged. Have it inspected by a certified chimney sweep.
Chimney fire damage isn't covered by the limited warranty.

safety.title: Safety around the stove
safety.html:
• Keep at least one smoke detector and one carbon monoxide monitor in the room with the stove, and more around the house. Don't disable or move them. If an alarm sounds, get everyone out right away.
  • Keep a fire extinguisher in a central spot that everyone in the house knows.
  • The stove is hot whenever it's running. Keep children and pets from touching it.
  • Keep anything that can burn, like clothing or furniture, at least 48" from the front. Don't store firewood within the clearances or in the space you need for loading and ash removal.
  • Run it with the door closed; open the door only to add wood.
  • Don't block the air openings or the space under the stove.
Surfaces, including the glass, stay hot long after the fire is out. Let the stove cool before any maintenance.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
The limited warranty covers the original purchaser of a stove bought from an authorized Blaze King dealer and installed in the USA or Canada. It starts on the purchase date and can't be transferred.

Catalytic combustor6 years · no charge years 1–3; you pay 60%, 70%, 80% in years 4–6
Stove body, accessories, steel firebox5 years · you pay 20%, 40%, 60%, 80% in years 2–5
Fan assemblies, thermostat, door handle steel parts2 years · parts + limited labor
All parts and materials, incl. paint1 year · parts + limited labor

Not covered, or voids it

  • Over-firing (warped plates, burnt-off paint)
  • Salt-saturated or treated wood, or any fuel other than cord wood
  • Gasket material and firebrick
  • Installs not to code, alteration, abuse, neglect, or damage in transit
Report a problem to your dealer within 30 days of noticing it, with proof and date of purchase. A failed combustor goes back to the dealer with a Combustor Failure Report.

Build fires directly on the bottom brick; no grate. Load fuel only in the usable loading area, which the manual showsas a shaded diagram on p. 24; loading beyond it voids the warranty. Cord wood only.

specFlue.title: Flue & connector
specFlue.html:
Flue collar opening8" I.D. (203 mm)
Flue pipe8" diameter, 24 MSG steel; no aluminum or galvanized
Chimneylisted factory-built, solid fuel, UL-103HT (USA) / CAN/ULC-S629 (CAN); or code-approved masonry with a flue liner
Close clearance / mobile home8" listed double wall close clearance connector + matching listed chimney

A chimney connector is required; don't install the chimney directly at the outlet. Keep the connector as direct aspossible and never pass it through an attic, roof space, closet, concealed space, floor or ceiling. Fasten all joints withsheet metal screws. Use a chimney support package at a ceiling connection to a prefab chimney and a listed wall thimblethrough a combustible wall. Double wall pipe from the stove top adaptor to the ceiling support box is recommended.

Never connect to a flue serving another appliance (voids warranty). Chimney temperatures in a creosote fire may exceed 2000F (1100°C).

specHeight.title: Chimney height
specHeight.html:
Minimum recommended height, stove top to termination, by elevation. Columns: no elbows / 2 x 15° / 2 x 30° / 2 x 45°.

0 - 1000 ft15 / 16 / 18 / 19 ft
1000 - 2000 ft15.5 / 16.5 / 18.5 / 19.5 ft
2000 - 3000 ft16 / 17 / 19 / 20 ft
3000 - 4000 ft16.5 / 17.5 / 19.5 / 20.5 ft
4000 - 5000 ft17 / 18 / 20 / 21 ft
5000 - 6000 ft17.5 / 18.5 / 20.5 / 21.5 ft
6000-7000 ft18 / 19 / 21 / 22 ft
7000 - 8000 ft18.5 / 19.5 / 21.5 / 22.5 ft

No more than one offset (two elbows); two 45° elbows equal one 90°. Add for other components: 90° elbow = 2.0 ft;"T" section = 3.0 ft; 1.0 ft of horizontal run = 2 ft of vertical rise. Manual's sea-level example: 15.0 + 2.0 (one 90°)+ 4.0 (2.0' horizontal run) + 3.0 (base "T") = 24.0 ft.

The chimney must also be at least 3ft above the highest point where it passes through the roof and 2ft above the highestpart of the roof or any obstruction within 10ft horizontally (p. 12). Wall exit: 3 ft of vertical from stove top to elbow isrecommended, with a pair of 45° elbows rather than one 90°. The manual calls these figures guidelines only and refers todraft performance (p. 11).

specClear.title: Clearances to combustibles
specClear.html:
Wall, corner and ceiling clearances are given as lettered dimensions (A–L) keyed to the clearance diagram on p. 10,repeated on the certification label (p. 4). Read them from that diagram; the residential (roof or wall exit) andmobile-home (roof exit only) rows carry identical values.

Combustible objects, front48" (1219 mm) minimum
Single wall pipe, Canada18" minimum

Install to all local codes; minimum clearances may only be reduced by means approved by the regulatory authority. Check local codes and the pipe manufacturer's specs for pipe clearances. Mobile home: Fan Kit or Rear Shield Kit plusOutside Air Kit required. The Rear Shield Kit (S.Z4710) is used to achieve minimum rear clearances (p. 16).

specFloor.title: Floor protection
specFloor.html:
No thermal hearth pad is required, but a combustible floor needs a non-combustible floor shield.

Minimum size, USA35" x 43.125" (889 x 1096 mm)
Minimum size, Canada47" x 53.125" (1194 x 1350 mm)
USA extension16" out from the front, 8" out from either side of the fuel-loading door
Canada (CSA B365)18" (450 mm) beyond any side with a door; 8" (200 mm) beyond other sides
Under the chimney connectorat least 2" either side

The shield needs no insulation value but must be listed under UL 1618-2009 (Type 1). In Canada the 18" door-side emberprotection spans the full width of the appliance plus the 8" each side; within 8" (200 mm) of a wall the pad need only reachthe base of the wall. Don't lay an ember pad on carpet unless it's structurally supported. Adhesive-based vinyl flooring infront of the stove isn't recommended; it can warp permanently.

conflicts.issue: Fan timing at start-up: lighting step 7 says turn fan(s) on to high once the door is latched and the bypass closed, and step 11 says turn the fan on after the initial warm up (p. 25); Fan Operation says fans should be off until the stove reaches normal operating temperatures, matching the thermostat setting about 30 minutes after the fire is established (p. 21).
Fan-off time before reading the catalytic thermometer: approximately 5 minutes (p. 23) vs 10 minutes (pp. 34, 40).

Catalytic Thermometer Maintenance gives owner steps to clean the probe and recalibrate the needle, but the next paragraph says any thermostat or thermometer maintenance must be completed by a certified installer (both p. 34).

Combustor part number: certification label gives combustor OEM part number 115-1510-C2 (p. 4); Combustor Warranty gives OEM Blaze King part # S.CAT40 and the parts list shows S.CAT40 Combustor Assembly (pp. 31, 42).
conflicts.reason: Two numbering systems: 115-1510-C2 is the combustor OEM part number printed on the certification label (p. 4); S.CAT40 is Blaze King's own part number for the combustor assembly (p. 31 'OEM Blaze King part #', parts list p. 42). The guide shows both and says what each is.

conflicts.issue: Fireplace installs: certification label says not to be installed in any fireplace (p. 4); Alcoves and Fireplaces bars alcove or fireplace installs in Canada and, for the USA, only says to adhere to minimum safe clearance dimensions (p. 15).

Mobile-home kits: Outside Air Kit plus either Fan Kit or Rear Shield Kit (pp. 4, 10, 15) vs the Optional Accessories list, which describes both the Rear Shield Kit and the Fan Kit as required for mobile home or alcove installations (p. 16).

review.notes: Single combined operation & installation manual (180-KE40 v3.01, 48 pp). Not transcribed because the meaning lives only in figures or the text is garbled: lettered wall/corner/ceiling clearances A-L and footnotes *1/*2 (pp. 4, 10; the text never says what each letter measures; the catalog clearances_note values 10/6/4/48-1/8 in match table values A, B, E, J but the manual can't confirm the labels); appliance dimension drawings (pp. 7-9, fractions garbled); usable loading-area diagram (p. 24); tested low-burn thermostat setting figure (p. 27, garbled); shoulder-season outdoor temperature range (p. 27, garbled); brick layout and fan parts (p. 43, partly garbled); warranty check-mark grid (p. 44), so the warranty drawer uses the prose terms on pp. 45-47. The manual gives no efficiency %, burn time or heating area, so catalog efficiency_pct 81, burn_time_hr_max 40 and heating area 1500-3000 could not be checked; catalog view_area (17 1/2 x 10 1/2 in) is not in the manual, which gives only a firebox door opening of 18 1/2" x 9 3/4". Catalog weight 420 lb matches the manual's shipping weight, firebox only. Minor metric inconsistency: 18" is given as 457 mm (p. 4), 456 mm (p. 10 lettered H/K) and 450 mm (p. 10 text); guide shows the inch value only. Parts list p. 42: door glass gasket S.155.0254.6 is described as 5 ft while the other gasket part suffixes match their lengths; worth a look. Reloading steps 2 and 3 (p. 26) both say to open the bypass; written once in the guide. The 'not in a sleeping room' rule appears in the mobile-home context on the label (p. 4) and p. 15; the guide attributes it to the label rather than stating its scope.
